title: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
summary: Decompose a monthly series, forecast it with naive, seasonal naive, exponential smoothing and Holt-Winters, then evaluate honestly with MASE and rolling origins before reaching for Prophet or foundation models.
outcomes: Explain why random train/test splits leak the future in time series and how rolling-origin evaluation avoids it
Compute a classical additive decomposition and naive, seasonal naive and SES forecasts by hand
Explain how alpha controls SES weights and why Holt-Winters adds trend and seasonal states
Compute MAE, RMSE, MAPE and MASE, and explain when MAPE breaks
Judge Prophet, ML and foundation models against simple baselines using the M4 evidence

lessons.title: Forecasting is supervised learning where the future is off limits

blocks.md:
A **time series** is a sequence of measurements taken at regular intervals: monthly sales, hourly air quality, daily active users. **Forecasting** means predicting future values $y_{T+1}, y_{T+2}, \dots$ from the history $y_1, \dots, y_T$. The number of steps ahead, $h$, is the **horizon**, and the last observed time $T$ is the **forecast origin**.

From the prerequisite course you know the recipe: pick a model, minimize a loss on training data, check for overfitting on held-out data. Forecasting is the same recipe where the inputs are **lagged** values of the series itself, such as last month $y_{t-1}$ or the same month last year $y_{t-12}$, and the label is $y_t$.

This course uses one toy series throughout so every number can be checked. It has 48 months built as $y_t = 100 + 2t + S_{\text{month}} + \text{noise}$, with $t$ counting from 0, a fixed seasonal pattern that peaks in July (+30) and bottoms in February and December (-25), and integer noise between -4 and 4. We stand at the end of month 36 and forecast months 37 to 48. The values of months 37 to 48 are the **test set**: we only look at them to score forecasts.

blocks.title: The toy monthly series: trend plus seasonality plus noise

scenes.caption: 48 monthly observations. The dashed line marks the forecast origin: months 1 to 36 are training data, months 37 to 48 are the test year we try to predict.
The series rises about 2 per month (the trend) and repeats the same shape every 12 months (the seasonality). Both patterns continue into the test year, so a good forecast must carry both forward.

blocks.md:
Why not split the 48 months at random into train and test, as you would for independent examples? Because neighboring months are strongly correlated. If month 40 is in the test set and months 39 and 41 are in training, the model can nearly read the answer off its neighbors.

In our series, estimating each of months 37 to 47 as the average of the month before and the month after gives a mean absolute error of only 5.09. That number says nothing about forecasting: at a real forecast origin you never have the month after.

A random train/test split on a time series leaks the future into training and makes every model look better than it will be in production. Hyndman and Athanasopoulos state the rule plainly: the training set may contain only observations that occurred before the test observations, so no future observations are used to construct the forecast.

Forecasting also differs from ordinary regression in one more way: the target is a whole path. A forecast made at $T$ for $h = 1, \dots, 12$ has errors that typically grow with $h$, so accuracy must always be reported together with the horizon it was measured at.

blocks.question: A teammate shuffles 5 years of daily demand data, holds out a random 20 percent of days, and reports a test error far below the error the model gets after deployment. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model is underfitting, so it needs more parameters
Random holdout days sit between training days, so the model effectively interpolated instead of forecasting
Daily data has too much noise to evaluate on 20 percent of days
The loss function should have been squared error instead of absolute error
blocks.explain: Held-out days surrounded by training days on both sides can be predicted from their neighbors, which is interpolation. In production the next day's neighbors are not yet observed. A split by time (train on the past, test on the future) measures the real task.

blocks.md: A forecast is a prediction made at an origin $T$ using only data up to $T$, for a stated horizon $h$. Every evaluation in this course respects that constraint.

lessons.title: Splitting a series into trend, season and remainder

blocks.md: Before forecasting, look at the structure. An **additive decomposition** writes each observation as a sum of three parts: a **trend-cycle** $T_t$ (the slow movement of the level), a **seasonal component** $S_t$ (a pattern that repeats with period $m$, here $m = 12$ months) and a **remainder** $R_t$ (whatever is left).

blocks.caption: Additive decomposition. A multiplicative version $y_t = S_t \times T_t \times R_t$ suits series whose seasonal swings grow with the level.

blocks.md:
**Classical decomposition**, a method from the 1920s, estimates the parts in four steps (FPP3 section 3.4):

1. Trend: for even $m$, take a $2 \times m$ moving average (MA), a centered 12-month average where the two end months get half weight.
2. Detrend: compute $y_t - \hat T_t$.
3. Season: average the detrended values of each month across years, then shift the 12 averages so they sum to zero.
4. Remainder: $\hat R_t = y_t - \hat T_t - \hat S_t$.

blocks.caption: The 2x12-MA. Each of the 12 months gets equal total weight, so the seasonal pattern cancels and the trend remains.

scenes.caption: Year 2 of the training data. The raw values mix a rising level with a summer peak, so neither pattern can be read off directly.
Step 1: the centered 2x12 moving average. It climbs smoothly from 123.2 to 145.0, about 2 per month, matching the trend we built in.
Step 2: subtract the trend. What is left swings from -28.0 in December to +34.8 in July: mostly season, plus noise.
Step 3: average each month's detrended values over the years where the MA exists, then center them to sum to zero. July becomes +31.5, December -28.0.
Step 4: remainder = y - trend - seasonal. All values lie within plus or minus 3.3, consistent with the noise of plus or minus 4 we added. The structure has been captured.

blocks.title: Estimated seasonal component vs the pattern we built in

scenes.caption: Top row: the seasonal indices from 36 months of training data. Bottom row: the pattern used to generate the series. They agree within about 3 in every month.
The largest misses are December (-28.0 vs -25), September (7.1 vs 10) and April (-2.6 vs 0): with only 2 detrended values per month, noise of plus or minus 4 still leaks into the averages.

blocks.prompt: The 2x12-MA needs 6 months on each side. Over the 36 training months, for how many months can classical decomposition estimate the trend?
blocks.reveal: Only 24: months 7 to 30. The first 6 and the last 6 months have no trend estimate and therefore no remainder either. FPP3 lists this as a weakness of classical decomposition, together with over-smoothing of sharp rises and falls, a seasonal pattern forced to repeat identically every year, and no robustness to unusual values.

blocks.md: For real work FPP3 recommends better methods, such as **STL** (Seasonal and Trend decomposition using Loess, Cleveland et al. 1990), which lets the seasonal pattern change over time, lets you control trend smoothness, and can be made robust to outliers. In Python it is `statsmodels.tsa.seasonal.STL`. Decomposition itself is descriptive; the next lessons turn these ideas into forecasts.

blocks.question: A city's electricity demand used to peak in winter (heating) and now peaks in summer (air conditioning). Which decomposition choice handles this best?
options: Classical decomposition, because it averages each month over all years
A larger moving-average window for the trend
STL with a seasonal component allowed to change over time
Multiplicative classical decomposition
blocks.explain: Classical decomposition assumes the same seasonal pattern every year, so it would average the old winter peak with the new summer peak. STL lets the seasonal component evolve, which is exactly what this series needs. FPP3 uses this electricity example to illustrate the limitation.

lessons.title: Naive, seasonal naive and simple exponential smoothing

blocks.md:
Every forecasting project starts with **benchmark methods** that need no fitting. FPP3 defines them precisely:

- **Naive**: every future value equals the last observation, $\hat y_{T+h|T} = y_T$. It is optimal when the data follow a random walk and works remarkably well for many economic and financial series.
- **Seasonal naive**: every future value equals the last observed value from the same season, for example next March equals last March.

The notation $\hat y_{T+h|T}$ reads: the forecast of $y_{T+h}$ made with data up to $T$.

blocks.caption: Seasonal naive. With $m = 12$ and $h \le 12$, $k = 0$, so the forecast for month $T+h$ is simply $y_{T+h-12}$.

blocks.title: Test year: actual values vs two baselines

scenes.caption: The 12 test months we try to forecast from the origin at month 36 (December of year 3, value 145).
Naive: all 12 forecasts equal 145, the last value. Errors grow from 2 in February to 73 in July because the naive method ignores both the summer peak and the upward trend. MAE = 455 / 12 = 37.92.
Seasonal naive: copy year 3 month by month. The shape now matches, and every error is between 19 and 30. MAE = 291 / 12 = 24.25.
All seasonal naive errors are positive: the forecasts are about a year of trend (12 x 2 = 24) too low. Seasonal naive captures the season but not the growth, which is its systematic bias here.

blocks.md: **Simple exponential smoothing** (SES) sits between two extremes: the naive method puts all weight on the last observation, while the mean method weights all history equally. SES uses a weighted average where weights decay geometrically with age, controlled by a **smoothing parameter** $0 \le \alpha \le 1$. Its component form keeps one state, the **level** $\ell_t$.

blocks.caption: Forecast equation and smoothing equation. Unrolled, the weight on $y_{T-j}$ is $\alpha(1-\alpha)^j$.

blocks.title: SES weight on an observation j months old

scenes.caption: alpha = 0.2: the newest value gets 0.2, then 0.16, 0.128, 0.102... Weight spreads over many months, so the level is smooth and slow to react.
alpha = 0.5: weights halve each month (0.5, 0.25, 0.125). The last 3 months carry 87.5 percent of the total weight.
alpha = 0.9: 0.9 on the last value, 0.09 on the one before, then almost nothing. SES has become nearly the naive method. Drag the slider to explore.

blocks.title: SES by hand on the first 5 months, alpha = 0.3
blocks.code:
alpha = 0.3
level = y[0]            # initial level l0 = first value
for t in range(5):
    fc = level            # one-step forecast
    err = y[t] - fc
    level = alpha * y[t] + (1 - alpha) * level

scenes.caption: Start with level = 81 (a common simple choice; statsmodels can also estimate l0).
Month 1: forecast 81, actual 81, error 0, level stays 81.
Month 2: forecast 81, actual 75, error -6. Level moves 30 percent of the way: 0.3 x 75 + 0.7 x 81 = 79.2.
Month 3: forecast 79.2, actual 96, error 16.8, new level 84.24.
Months 4 and 5: errors 17.76 and 25.43, all positive. The level lags behind a rising series, which is what a model with no trend term does.

blocks.md: Like regression, $\alpha$ (and $\ell_0$) can be chosen by minimizing the in-sample sum of squared one-step errors, $\text{SSE} = \sum_t (y_t - \hat y_{t|t-1})^2$. In statsmodels this is `SimpleExpSmoothing(y).fit()`, or `fit(smoothing_level=0.3)` to fix the value.

blocks.title: Choosing alpha on the 36 training months (l0 = 81)

scenes.caption: In-sample one-step SSE (in thousands) by alpha: 28.1, 18.4, 15.0, 10.6, 7.7, 6.1, 5.7. A grid search over 0.01 to 1.00 picks alpha = 1.0, the naive method.
Test MAE over the 12-month horizon by alpha: 32.19, 26.06, 26.26, 30.53, 34.68, 37.21, 37.92. The alpha that best predicts one step ahead is the worst here.

blocks.prompt: Why does the SSE-optimal alpha on this series go all the way to 1?
blocks.reveal: With a strong trend and season, last month is the best single guess for this month, so one-step error falls as SES copies the last value more closely. SES has no trend or season term, so it cannot do better than chase the data. FPP3 notes its forecasts are flat ($\hat y_{T+h|T} = \ell_T$) and suitable only for series without trend or seasonality. A small alpha happened to help over 12 steps because averaging over a full year lands near the yearly mean, which is closer to next year's values than the December low of 145.

blocks.md: A parameter fitted to minimize one-step in-sample error is not automatically good at the horizon you care about. Always evaluate at the real horizon on data the fit never saw.

blocks.question: On the test year, seasonal naive has MAE 24.25 and naive has MAE 37.92. What would most directly remove seasonal naive's remaining error on this series?
options: Use a smaller alpha
Switch from MAE to RMSE
Use only the last 12 months of training data
Add a trend term, since all its errors are positive by roughly one year of growth
blocks.explain: Every seasonal naive error is positive, between 19 and 30, close to 12 months x 2 per month = 24. That is a systematic bias from ignoring the trend. A method with both trend and season terms (Holt-Winters, next lesson) addresses it. Changing the metric changes the score, not the forecast.

lessons.title: Holt-Winters and ARIMA: models with trend and season

blocks.md: Exponential smoothing was proposed in the late 1950s (Brown 1959, Holt 1957, Winters 1960). Holt extended SES with a **trend** state $b_t$ (the slope), and Holt and Winters extended that with a **seasonal** state $s_t$. The resulting **Holt-Winters additive method** has three smoothing equations with parameters $\alpha$, $\beta^*$ and $\gamma$, each a weighted average between a new estimate and the old one, exactly like SES.

blocks.tex: \begin{aligned}\hat y_{t+h|t} &= \ell_t + h b_t + s_{t+h-m(k+1)} \\ \ell_t &= \alpha(y_t - s_{t-m}) + (1-\alpha)(\ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1}) \\ b_t &= \beta^*(\ell_t - \ell_{t-1}) + (1-\beta^*) b_{t-1} \\ s_t &= \gamma(y_t - \ell_{t-1} - b_{t-1}) + (1-\gamma) s_{t-m}\end{aligned}
blocks.caption: Holt-Winters additive method (FPP3 section 8.3). The level update uses the seasonally adjusted observation; the season update compares the observation with the level plus trend.

blocks.md: Read each line as a smoothing step. The level blends the deseasonalized observation with where last period's level and slope pointed. The slope blends the newest level change with the old slope. The seasonal index for this month blends this year's deviation with last year's index. The forecast adds the level, $h$ steps of slope, and the most recent index for the target month. Use the **additive** form when seasonal swings stay roughly constant, and the **multiplicative** form when they grow with the level.

blocks.title: Holt-Winters additive vs seasonal naive on the test year

scenes.caption: Seasonal naive, from the previous lesson: correct shape, every month about 24 too low. MAE 24.25.
Holt-Winters additive (alpha 0.7, beta* 0, gamma 0.55): the slope lifts every month, and the July forecast is 206.1 vs actual 218. MAE drops to 7.49.

Simplified model: initial states from the first two years, parameters from a 0.05-step grid on one-step SSE, without FPP3's usual limit gamma at most 1 - alpha. statsmodels also estimates initial states, so its parameters and MAE differ.

blocks.code:
from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import ExponentialSmoothing

# y: pandas Series of the 36 training months
fit = ExponentialSmoothing(
    y, trend="add", seasonal="add", seasonal_periods=12
).fit()                      # estimates alpha, beta, gamma and initial states
print(fit.params["smoothing_level"])
forecast = fit.forecast(12)  # months 37 to 48
blocks.caption: Holt-Winters in statsmodels. trend and seasonal accept "add" or "mul"; damped_trend=True damps the slope over long horizons.

blocks.md: The second classic family is **ARIMA**. A series is **stationary** when its statistical properties do not depend on when you look at it; trend and seasonality break stationarity. **Differencing**, $y'_t = y_t - y_{t-1}$, removes a trend, and seasonal differencing $y_t - y_{t-12}$ removes a stable season. ARIMA then models the differenced series with an **autoregression** (AR, a regression on its own lags) plus a **moving average** term (MA, a regression on past one-step errors $\varepsilon$).

blocks.caption: ARIMA(p, d, q): p AR lags, d rounds of differencing, q MA lags. Integrated means the reverse of differencing. Seasonal ARIMA adds the same terms at lag m.

blocks.md: The two families overlap. FPP3 lists exact equivalences: the naive method is ARIMA(0,1,0), and SES with additive errors, ETS(A,N,N), is ARIMA(0,1,1) with $\theta_1 = \alpha - 1$. FPP3 calls it a myth that ARIMA is more general: linear exponential smoothing models are special cases of ARIMA, but nonlinear (multiplicative) exponential smoothing models have no ARIMA counterpart, and some ARIMA models have no smoothing counterpart. In Python, `statsmodels.tsa.arima.model.ARIMA(y, order=(p, d, q), seasonal_order=(P, D, Q, m))` fits one.

blocks.prompt: The fitted Holt-Winters model chose beta* = 0. Does that mean the model has no trend?
blocks.reveal: No. beta* = 0 means the slope is never updated after initialization, so the model keeps a fixed slope, here the initial estimate (year 2 mean minus year 1 mean) / 12 = 1.98 per month. Because the true trend in this series really is constant (2 per month), never changing the slope is a sensible choice. A nonzero beta* lets the slope drift when growth speeds up or slows down.

blocks.question: Which statement about ARIMA and exponential smoothing is correct according to FPP3?
options: SES is equivalent to ARIMA(0,1,1), but multiplicative exponential smoothing models have no ARIMA equivalent
ARIMA strictly contains every exponential smoothing model
ARIMA cannot model seasonality
Exponential smoothing models are all stationary
blocks.explain: Linear (additive) ETS models map to ARIMA forms, for example ETS(A,N,N) to ARIMA(0,1,1). Nonlinear ETS models have no ARIMA counterpart, and all ETS models are nonstationary while some ARIMA models are stationary. Seasonal ARIMA handles seasonality with seasonal lags and differencing.

blocks.question: A product's monthly seasonal swing is about 10 units when sales are 100, and about 50 units when sales are 500. Which Holt-Winters variant fits best?
options: Additive seasonality
No seasonal component, with a damped trend
Multiplicative seasonality
Seasonal naive with a 6-month period
blocks.explain: The seasonal swing scales with the level (10 percent of sales), which is the case FPP3 gives for the multiplicative method. Additive seasonality assumes a constant swing in absolute units.

lessons.title: Honest evaluation: error metrics, MASE and rolling origins

blocks.md:
A forecast **error** is $e_{T+h} = y_{T+h} - \hat y_{T+h|T}$, computed on test data. It differs from a **residual**, which is a one-step error on the training data. Four common summaries (FPP3 section 5.8):

- **MAE**, mean of $|e_t|$: in the units of the data. Minimizing it leads to forecasts of the median.
- **RMSE**, $\sqrt{\text{mean}(e_t^2)}$: also in data units, punishes large errors more, and leads to forecasts of the mean.
- **MAPE**, mean of $|100\, e_t / y_t|$: unit free, but with pitfalls.
- **MASE**: errors scaled by a naive benchmark's in-sample error.

scenes.caption: MAE: 37.92, 24.25, 37.92, 26.26, 7.49. SES with its fitted alpha = 1 is identical to naive.
RMSE: 42.96, 24.51, 42.96, 31.12, 8.57. Naive's RMSE is far above its MAE because its errors are uneven (2 to 73). Seasonal naive's errors are nearly constant, so its RMSE is close to its MAE.
MAPE in percent: 19.72, 13.49, 19.72, 13.58, 4.12. Same ranking here, but percentages hide a trap shown below.
MASE: 1.566, 1.002, 1.566, 1.085, 0.310. Below 1 means better than the in-sample seasonal naive. Only Holt-Winters is clearly below 1.

blocks.md: **MAPE pitfalls**. It is infinite or undefined when any $y_t = 0$ and explodes when $y_t$ is near zero: actual 1, forecast 3 gives 200 percent. It assumes the unit has a meaningful zero, so it is meaningless for temperature in Celsius. And it penalizes over-forecasts more than under-forecasts of the same size: actual 50, forecast 100 is 100 percent, while actual 100, forecast 50 is 50 percent. The so-called symmetric MAPE (sMAPE) is still unstable near zero and can even be negative; Hyndman and Koehler (2006) recommend not using it.

**MASE** (Hyndman and Koehler 2006) fixes the scale problem differently: divide each test error by the training-set MAE of a one-step benchmark. For seasonal data the benchmark is seasonal naive, so the scale $Q$ is the average of $|y_t - y_{t-m}|$ over the training data.

blocks.caption: With $m = 1$ the denominator is the naive one-step MAE, used for nonseasonal series.

blocks.title: MASE by hand: the scale from 24 seasonal differences

scenes.caption: T = 36 and m = 12, so there are 36 - 12 = 24 seasonal differences in the training data. Year 2 vs year 1 sums to 285; year 3 vs year 2 sums to 296.
Scale Q = (285 + 296) / 24 = 581 / 24 = 24.21. On average, last year's same month missed by 24.21 inside the training data.
Seasonal naive test errors sum to 291, so MAE = 24.25 and MASE = 24.25 / 24.21 = 1.002: as good out of sample as it was in sample.

The same scale serves every method: naive MASE = 37.92 / 24.21 = 1.566, Holt-Winters MASE = 7.49 / 24.21 = 0.310. Because Q is in the same units as the errors, MASE is unit free and compares across series.

blocks.md: One test year is one sample. **Time series cross-validation**, also called **rolling-origin evaluation**, repeats the forecast from several origins. Each training set contains only data before its test window, and successive training sets grow (scikit-learn's `TimeSeriesSplit` produces the same pattern: each training set is a superset of the previous one). Below, origins are months 24, 30, 36 and 42, each with a 6-month horizon, and every model is refitted at each origin.

scenes.caption: Fold 1: train on months 1 to 24, forecast months 25 to 30.
Fold 2: the origin moves to month 30. The training window grows; months 25 to 30, the previous test window, are now training data.
Folds 3 and 4 complete the pattern. Every test window lies strictly after its training data, and together they cover months 25 to 48.

blocks.title: MASE per origin (horizon 6), each fold scaled by its own training data

scenes.caption: Origin 24 (Dec): naive 1.305, seasonal naive 1.018, Holt-Winters 0.689.
Origin 30 (Jun): naive 0.656 beats seasonal naive 1.053. From June the next 6 months start high and fall, so holding June's value is a lucky fit this time.
Origin 36 (Dec): naive 1.122, seasonal naive 0.998, Holt-Winters 0.402.
Origin 42 (Jun): naive 0.606 again beats seasonal naive 1.006.
Average over 4 origins: naive 0.922, seasonal naive 1.019, Holt-Winters 0.438. The naive vs seasonal naive ranking depends on where the origin falls; only Holt-Winters wins at every origin.

blocks.md: Report a forecast's accuracy as an average over many origins, at the horizon you will use in production, with a scaled metric such as MASE next to seasonal naive. A single train/test split can rank two methods either way by luck.

blocks.question: Sales of a niche product are 0 in some weeks. A dashboard compares models by MAPE. What goes wrong, and what is a better choice?
options: Nothing, MAPE handles zeros by skipping them
MAPE becomes negative, so use sMAPE instead
MAPE overweights large values, so use RMSE on percentages
MAPE is undefined when actuals are 0 and explodes near 0, so use a scaled metric such as MASE
blocks.explain: Percentage errors divide by $y_t$, so a zero actual makes the error infinite or undefined and small actuals dominate the average. MASE divides by the in-sample naive or seasonal naive MAE instead, which is nonzero unless the training series is constant (or, for the seasonal scale, repeats exactly every season). sMAPE is not recommended either.

blocks.question: A model has MASE 0.8 on a monthly test set, scaled by the in-sample seasonal naive MAE. What does that mean?
options: Its errors are 20 percent smaller on average than the seasonal naive one-step errors measured on the training data
Its MAPE is 80 percent
It is correct 80 percent of the time
It is 0.8 units off on average
blocks.explain: MASE is the test MAE divided by the training MAE of seasonal naive one-step forecasts. Below 1 means smaller average errors than that benchmark achieved in sample; above 1 means larger.

lessons.title: Prophet, the M4 competition and foundation models

blocks.md: **Prophet** was introduced by Sean Taylor and Ben Letham at Facebook in the paper *Forecasting at Scale*, aimed at many business series and analysts without deep time-series expertise. FPP3 describes it as a nonlinear regression $y_t = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + \varepsilon_t$: a piecewise-linear trend $g$ with automatically chosen changepoints (optionally logistic, with a cap), seasonal terms $s$ built from Fourier series (default order 10 for yearly and 3 for weekly), holiday dummies $h$, and Bayesian estimation.

The Prophet documentation says it works best with strong seasonal effects and several seasons of history, and is robust to missing data and trend shifts. FPP3's own comparisons are more cautious: on quarterly cement production, Prophet was worse than both ETS and ARIMA, and the authors conclude that it is fast and fully automated but rarely gives better accuracy than the alternatives in their examples. Treat it like any other candidate: run it through the same rolling-origin evaluation against seasonal naive.

The **M competitions**, organized by Spyros Makridakis, test methods on large collections of real series. M4 (2018) used 100,000 series and 61 methods, scored point forecasts with sMAPE and MASE, and reported five major findings:

1. Of the 17 most accurate methods, 12 were combinations of mostly statistical approaches.
2. The biggest surprise was a hybrid of statistical and machine learning features, close to 10 percent more accurate (sMAPE) than the combination benchmark.
3. The second best combined seven statistical methods and one ML method, with weights learned by an ML model.
4. The two best methods also produced accurate 95 percent prediction intervals.
5. The six pure ML methods performed poorly: none beat the combination benchmark (the average of SES, Holt and damped exponential smoothing), and only one beat Naive2 (naive applied to seasonally adjusted data).

blocks.title: The M4 winner: exponential smoothing inside a neural network

nodes.label:
global dilated LSTM
shared by all series

RNN output x level
x seasonality

scenes.caption: Slawek Smyl's winning M4 entry (ES-RNN) is hybrid: per-series smoothing parameters and seasonality, inspired by multiplicative Holt-Winters, plus one neural network shared by all series.
Simplified view: the smoothing level and seasonality divide out of each input window, so the network sees deseasonalized, normalized windows from every series.
The network predicts the whole horizon, which is multiplied by the level and seasonality. All parameters, per-series and global, are fitted together by gradient descent.

blocks.md: **Foundation models** are the newest entry. **Chronos** (Ansari et al., 2024) scales and quantizes series values into a fixed vocabulary of tokens and trains T5-family language models (20M to 710M parameters) with cross-entropy, on public data plus synthetic Gaussian-process series. On 42 datasets it beat other methods on datasets seen in training and was comparable, occasionally better, **zero-shot** (no training on the target data) on new ones. **TimesFM** (Das et al., 2023) is a decoder-only attention model over patches of the series whose zero-shot accuracy approaches supervised models trained per dataset. These are useful when you have many series and little time to tune, but the evaluation rules do not change.

Misconception: a bigger or newer model will beat simple methods. On the M4 data pure ML lost to simple combinations, and on our toy series SES with a fitted alpha was no better than naive. Any model, from Prophet to a foundation model, has to beat seasonal naive under rolling-origin evaluation before it ships.

scenes.caption: Start by looking: plot the series and decompose it to see trend, season and outliers. Then compute the free baselines.
Add classic statistical models next. They are fast, well understood and often hard to beat.
Only then try heavier models. Every candidate goes through the same rolling-origin evaluation, and the winner or a combination of the top few ships.

blocks.question: An ML team's global gradient-boosting model beats ARIMA on a single holdout month, but loses to seasonal naive on average across 12 rolling origins. What should ship?
options: The ML model, because it won the most recent month
ARIMA, because it is a statistical model
Seasonal naive, or a combination tested the same way, because it is best across origins
Nothing, because the metrics disagree
blocks.explain: One month is one sample; the average over 12 origins is the stronger evidence. If a cheap baseline wins under rolling-origin evaluation, ship it, or test a combination of methods, which M4 found to be consistently strong.

blocks.question: What does zero-shot forecasting with Chronos mean?
options: Forecasting with zero horizon
Forecasting a series the model was not trained on, without fitting to it
Training on zero-valued series only
Using no seasonal component
blocks.explain: Chronos is pretrained on a large corpus. Zero-shot means applying it directly to a new series with no training on that dataset. The Chronos paper reports comparable and occasionally better accuracy than models trained on those datasets.
